newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Asia financiers urge faster market development.
newsitem.headline: Asia financiers urge faster market development.

text.p: Top Asia Pacific financiers urged their governments on Saturday to speed up development of the region's financial markets to help attract the more than $1 trillion needed for economic development.
But it was not clear how finance ministers from the 18-strong Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) group would respond to the call at their weekend meeting at this luxury resort.
"It's easy enough to see the urgency of the tasks before us," Philippine President Fidel Ramos told the ministers. "It is harder to act upon them."

In a briefing for reporters, the financiers set out a series of concrete steps for the governments to take -- from the establishment of regional information centres on financing needs to the creation of bond rating agencies.

The aim of the exercise: to attract the $1.5 trillion that the developing economies of the region will need over the next decade to build the roads, telecommunication links and other infrastructure vital to a modern economy.

"There is no point for any economy to start talking about being a tiger economy when the growl of the tiger cannot be heard because it would take 10 calls between two telephone companies," said Johnny Ravalo, chief economist of the Bankers Association of the Philippines.

APEC comprises Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.

The focus here on concrete steps to promote financial market development was in a sense a reflection of how far the region -- and the investors who put money in it -- have evolved over the past few years.
Rather than taking fright and yanking money out of the region when the U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates late last month, investors responded calmly and there was little market turbulence.

"The investors are more sophisticated and the markets more mature," said Robert Hormats, vice chairman of Goldman Sachs (International) of New York. "The rhythms of the markets are different," he added.
Many of the financiers' recommendations involved steps to promote development of fully fledged capital markets throughout the region.

Hormats said that was because the region is likely to face greater difficulty raising debt finance through the issuance of long-term bonds and the like than in raising equity finance on local stock markets.
"The development of domestic bond markets is viewed as essential," the financiers said. "This voluntary initiative must be treated as a priority."
The financiers also complained of the treatment that global bank regulators accord developing country debt.

Those regulations -- which determine how much and what type of capital banks must set aside to cover their loans -- mean that the cost of capital for developing country borrowers is five times more than for their industrial country counterparts, Ravalo said.
Among the financiers' other recommendations: cross-listing of securities on various stock markets and standardization of accounting principles that companies must follow.
Hormats said finance ministers were likely to welcome many of the suggestions, but added that it remained unclear how rapidly they would act on them.
"They all want to move," he said. "Some of them just have constraints on how quickly they can go."
